newsitem.title: USA: Grigsby Brandford should survive - former chairman.
newsitem.headline: Grigsby Brandford should survive - former chairman.

text.p: The largest minority-owned investment banking firm in the U.S., Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc, will undergo significant downsizing, but should survive in some form, its former chairman said on Thursday.

Napoleon Brandford, who left Grigsby Brandford this week to develop Muriel Siebert & Co Inc's municipal finance business, told Reuters that many of Grigsby Brandford's clients planned to follow him to Muriel Siebert.
Brandford said Grigsby Brandford would lose many of its clients and employees, but added he does not expect the firm to file for dissolution, at least not at this time.
Brandford said his new municipal finance firm -- Siebert, Brandford, Shank & Co -- was likely to hire at least 30 employees away from Grigsby Brandford.
Brandford added that he expected "a significant number of Grigsby Brandford's existing clients to remain loyal to those who will join the new firm."

Brandford said he was already in contact with Grigsby Brandford clients about moving their business. A "significant number" of these clients have already committed to making the move. Brandford, however, declined to name the clients he will bring to Muriel Siebert.
"A month from now or less, Siebert, Brandford, Shank will look a lot like Grigsby Brandford's public finance effort," Brandford said in a telephone interview in San Francisco.
Negotiations over the future of Grigsby Brandford were underway, he said. Brandford declined to discuss the talks.
"The owners haven't decided what they're going to do yet," Brandford said. "But the firm has not and does not plan at this point to file for dissolution."
The changes at the firm will be profound, Brandford said. "It's a weaker firm today," he said. "Clearly it won't be the player it had been before."
But Brandford said; "The firm is still doing business and has over $3-plus million dollars in net capital."
The management shake-up at Grigsby Brandford began on September 17, when Calvin Grigsby, the firm's founder and long-time chairman, announced his resignation.
Grigsby resigned shortly after it was disclosed that authorities were investigating bond deals the firm handled in Dade County, Fla. Grigsby has not been charged with any wrongdoing in the probe.
In a statement issued on September 27, Grigsby's attorney said his client "strongly maintains his innocence."

"You may rest assured that we will do everything within our power to see that no charges are filed and, if they are filed, we will vigorously fight them," said attorney Johnnie Cochran, who is representing Grigsby.

Earlier this week, the shake-up at Grigsby Brandford intensified with the departure of Brandford and Suzanne Shank, who also joined New York-based Muriel Siebert & Co. After Grigsby left, shareholders of Grigsby Brandford appointed Brandford chairman of the board of directors and Shank president and chief executive officer.
Brandford said he left Grigsby Brandford in large part because the Florida probe made it "increasingly difficult to do business."
"It was unfair because of the maximum amount of exposure given to this issue when Calvin Grigsby hadn't been charged with anything," Brandford said.
